---

### Site and data used

| Item | Value | Source |
|------|--------|--------|
| Site | Elephants By The Lake (EBTL), ~68–70 acres (~28 ha) | [ebtl.earth](https://ebtl.earth/) |
| Location | Plus Code **7J4WP5MM+H9**, Budhimutlu / Chinna Tammaradapalli, Krishnagiri, TN 635121 | Site footer; Nominatim reverse geocode |
| Coordinates | **12.734°N, 78.183°E** | Open Location Code decode of `P5MM+H9` |
| Habitats | N: percolation ponds, wetland, panchayat lake; mid: living space, nursery/garden; S: restoration/wild zones next to Veppanapalli RF | [EBTL site map](https://ebtl.earth/static/images/ebtl-map-new.png) |
| Satellite check | Central tank/lake, small N pond, open scrub W/N, denser cover SE | ESRI World Imagery export around the Plus Code |

---

### Why public DBs look empty (but frogs are there)

**GBIF (Anura, research-grade / indexed occurrences):**

- **0** records within **2 km** of the Plus Code  
- **16** within **5 km**, **18** within **10 km**, **69** within **25 km**  
- Nearby species pool: *Hoplobatrachus tigerinus*, *Uperodon taprobanicus*, *Uperodon systoma*, *Uperodon variegatus*, *Sphaerotheca rolandae/breviceps*, *Euphlyctis cyanophlyctis*, *Polypedates maculatus*, *Microhyla ornata/rubra*, *Minervarya agricola*, *Duttaphrynus melanostictus*  
- Query: `https://api.gbif.org/v1/occurrence/search` with `taxonKey=952` and `geoDistance=12.733937,78.183437,{r}km`

**iNaturalist (Amphibia, all grades):**

- **5** obs within **0.5 km**, **8** within **2 km** — including on-campus  
- Examples on/near site: *Minervarya agricola* at place guess **P5MM+H9** ([obs 332000489](https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/332000489)); *Microhyla ornata*, *Uperodon systoma*, *Polypedates maculatus* within ~0.3–0.4 km (Aug–Dec 2024–2025)  
- Most are `needs_id`, so they **do not** flow into GBIF research-grade — that is why GBIF looks empty inside the fence

So sparse public records ≠ low occupancy; they reflect few research-grade uploads and nocturnal under-sampling.

---

### Occupancy estimate (method you can re-run)

**1. Map area (schematic)**  
On the published EBTL map, wetland/teal aquatic pixels were ~**15%** of mapped land colors → **~4.3 ha (~11 acres)** if applied to 69 acres. Aquatic cover is concentrated in the **northern third** of the elongated site (south ≈ dry restoration).

**2. Ecological buffer (dry-zone anurans)**  
Eastern Ghats / Deccan dry-deciduous frogs cluster on standing water and use a short terrestrial halo (litter, bunds, shrubs), especially after rain ([Gingee Hills inventory](http://www.ajcb.in/journals/full_papers_july_2018/AJCB-Vol7-No1-Karthik%20et%20al.pdf); Nallamala habitat typology; Meghamalai dry-forest anuran lists).  

Treating wetland+lake ≈ **3.5–4.5 ha** core, plus a **50–100 m** activity buffer, yields roughly **8–12 ha** of high-use habitat ≈ **29–43%** of the property — nearly all **north of the nursery / learning centre**.

**3. Seasonal nuance**

| Zone | Approx. share of site | Frog use |
|------|----------------------|----------|
| Wetland + percolation ponds + lake | ~10–15% | Core breeding / calling; year-round if water holds |
| N terrestrial fringe (≤~100 m from water), nursery irrigation | ~15–25% | Night foraging, calling from edges |
| Mid campus (lights, drains) | small | Opportunistic (*Duttaphrynus*, *Polypedates*) |
| S restoration / wild | ~½ of site | Low in dry months; **burrowing frogs after monsoon rain** |

**Verdict to use in planning:** report **~⅓ of the site occupied under normal wet-season nights**, with **breeding effectively confined to the northern aquatic complex (~⅛ of area)**. Do not treat the whole 70 acres as frog habitat.

---

### Where next night surveys should go (priority order)

1. **Panchayat lake shoreline** — full circuit; focus shallow, vegetated, and muddy edges (*Hoplobatrachus*, *Euphlyctis*, *Minervarya*).  
2. **Wetland interior + three percolation ponds** (north tip) — walk slowly; listen for *Microhyla* / *Uperodon*; check for eggs/tadpoles.  
3. **Wetland–campus ecotone** (learning centre / living space drains and lit edges) — short station for *Duttaphrynus* and *Polypedates*.  
4. **Nursery / food-garden irrigation margins** after watering or rain — *Minervarya*, small microhylids.  
5. **Only after heavy rain:** southern restoration patches and **SE edge toward Veppanapalli RF** — *Sphaerotheca*, *Uperodon* emerging from burrows; *Polypedates* on shrubs.

**Protocol (checkable):** time-constrained visual encounter + acoustic (e.g. 3–4 × 30–45 min stations), **19:00–23:00**, peak from local phenology **Aug–Nov** (matches on-site iNat dates). Record presence by station, water permanence, and GPS — then you can replace this habitat prior with an empirical occupancy model. Upload research-grade IDs so GBIF catches up.

---

### Bottom line

Frogs at EBTL are a **northern aquatic problem**, not a whole-property one: expect **~10–15% core water habitat** and **~25–40% regular night-use area**. Put survey effort on the **lake–wetland–pond complex first**; use the southern wild zones mainly as **post-rain** secondary transects.The background habitat run finished successfully: on the EBTL schematic map, aquatic/wetland colors were about **15%** of mapped land (~**4.3 ha** of the ~69-acre site), concentrated in the north. That underpins the occupancy estimate already given — frogs mainly use the northern lake–wetland–pond complex, so night surveys should start there.

Asian elephants function as ecosystem engineers by creating water-filled footprints that serve as critical breeding sites and nurseries for anurans [1][2][3]. These ephemeral, predator-free ponds provide stable habitat during the dry season when other water sources are unavailable, and they can persist for over a year [1][2][4]. Additionally, these trackways act as stepping stones across the landscape, facilitating connectivity, dispersal, and gene flow between otherwise fragmented frog populations [1][5][4]. Asian elephant dung has also been documented providing habitat for various frog species in dry environments [6].

Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) - A forest restoration project in the Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu

Over decades, the dry deciduous forests of our country have been stripped and exploited for commercial use. As native forests receded to only higher elevations of hills, creatures of the forests have also lost their footing in the valley. EBTL lies in one of those valleys. In the foothills of a degraded forest.

These 70 acres now 'belong' to us. How wonderful would it be if the other creatures also echoed the same thought? Our goal is to help the forest regain its rich biodiversity.

The year we began work, a few elephants came to the land, something that had never happened in the last many decades. We decided to call this project.

# Elephants By The Lake!

# The map of EBTL

Once you step into the hills around EBTL there are remnants of a once thriving forest; bird calls, fresh bear tracks, the jumping away of a troupe of langurs, trees in bloom or seed, spiders waiting for a catch, the scuffling across of a monitor lizard, a bird of prey gliding above.

Unfortunately this biodiverse ecosystem of the Eastern Ghats has been almost eradicated in terms of its area, but for a few hilly pockets where the tough terrain has made it too difficult for people to interfere.

Hopefully in time, the land will begin a cycle of regeneration where at a point, this space can become a safe corner for some of the rarer and threatened flora of the Eastern Ghats to flourish and wildlife can reinhabit the land.

# What happens at EBTL

#### Forest restoration

EBTL, primarily is focused on the native flora of the dry decidious forests of the South Deccan plateau.

#### Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies

We have established a dedicated in-house field research initiative at our campus in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, to address critical gaps in knowledge about Eastern Ghats biodiversity, ecology, and conservation priorities.

#### Organic farming

A small percentage of land we own is allotted for farming where we grow paddy, pulses, millets and vegetables.

#### Farmer's Collective

We work very closely with the nearby village of Chinnathamandrapalli. The villagers play a vital role in all the work we undertake. We have enabled a collective of women working towards value added products. They also manage our farm lands and campus.

# Farmer's Collective

We promote land stewardship and sustainable farming by employing the local community and supporting a farmers collective to create value-added products. Our goal is to provide eco-friendly job opportunities to counter urban migration among the younger generation.

# In-House Research at EBTL

The Eastern Ghats are among the oldest mountain systems on Earth, with geological origins tracing back to the Precambrian era. Yet, despite their age and ecological significance, the Eastern Ghats remain one of India’s least studied landscapes, especially when compared to the Western Ghats.

Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) has established a dedicated in-house field research initiative at our campus in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, to address critical gaps in knowledge about Eastern Ghats biodiversity, ecology, and conservation priorities.

# Our Research Focus

Our work begins with intensive field-based studies on herpetofauna and arachnids, groups that act as sensitive indicators of ecosystem health. Over time, the program will expand to include comprehensive biodiversity documentation across multiple taxa, creating a long-term ecological baseline for the region.

# Integrated, Science-Driven Approaches

EBTL’s research integrates multiple scientific disciplines, including:

- Field surveys and long-term ecological monitoring
- Molecular genetics and taxonomy
- Stable isotope ecology
- Spatial and landscape-level analysis

Together, these approaches generate robust, policy-relevant data that support:

- Conservation planning and habitat restoration
- IUCN Red List assessments
- Key Biodiversity Area (KBA) identification and designation

# Building Knowledge, Capacity, and Community

Our in-house research program is designed as a five-year initiative, focusing not only on science, but also on people and place. Key components include:

- Development of on-site research infrastructure
- Capacity building through an Open Taxonomic Initiative for students and early-career researchers
- Meaningful community engagement rooted in local ecological knowledge

# Why the Eastern Ghats Matter

Through sustained research, collaboration, and open data sharing, EBTL aims to help reposition the Eastern Ghats as a globally significant biodiversity landscape, deserving focused conservation action and international attention.

This initiative reflects our belief that effective conservation begins with deep, place-based understanding, grounded in rigorous science and strong local partnerships.

We brought in many cups of cultured water from different lakes to inoculate it with local fresh water microbiome, for the beneficial bacteria to outcompete the algae. 

There still was an algal bloom. We waited patiently for the snail population to scavenge algae and other dead organic matter. But instead, they were chomping down a lot of the new aquatic plants. 

We sat tight and waited for nature to occupy it's niches. Suddenly we saw the aquatic plants shoot past the size that the snails fancied and made them turn back to algae instead. We now had new babies of guppies, thalias, lilies and snails. 

It took a couple of years to see toads take to an urban pond inside a compound wall across the busiest street in malleshwaram. Frogs, dragonflies and damselflies were out of question, since they are nearly extinct in urban areas but Water bugs, Striders and Fishing spiders occupied every niche. The pond climaxed to a thriving clear water ecosystem that didn't need any interference from us, whatsoever. No topping up, no aeration, no de weeding.

Ponds are living, breathing ecosystems. Ananas folks love nothing more than to sit around a fresh water pond for hours. A lot of our work hours went into gazing at the glistening guppy tails catch the morning light and welcoming every new species of fresh water insects. 

Until last week, when the garden door was accidentally left open and the pest control sprayer walked in to our little regenerative garden and sprayed everything in a matter of minutes. 
Three minutes and a few ml of pyrethrin is all it takes to obliterate entire food chains of an ecosystem. (Contd. In comments)"</title>

Restoration Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies Livelihoods Project About Gallery

Over decades, the dry deciduous forests of our country have been stripped and exploited for commercial use. As native forests receded to only higher elevations of hills, creatures of the forests have also lost their footing in the valley. EBTL lies in one of those valleys. In the foothills of a degraded forest.

These 70 acres now 'belong' to us. How wonderful would it be if the other creatures also echoed the same thought? Our goal is to help the forest regain its rich biodiversity.

The year we began work, a few elephants came to the land, something that had never happened in the last many decades. We decided to call this project.

Elephants By The Lake!

The map of EBTL

Once you step into the hills around EBTL there are remnants of a once thriving forest; bird calls, fresh bear tracks, the jumping away of a troupe of langurs, trees in bloom or seed, spiders waiting for a catch, the scuffling across of a monitor lizard, a bird of prey gliding above.

Unfortunately this biodiverse ecosystem of the Eastern Ghats has been almost eradicated in terms of its area, but for a few hilly pockets where the tough terrain has made it too difficult for people to interfere.

Hopefully in time, the land will begin a cycle of regeneration where at a point, this space can become a safe corner for some of the rarer and threatened flora of the Eastern Ghats to flourish and wildlife can reinhabit the land.

What happens at EBTL

Forest restoration

EBTL, primarily is focused on the native flora of the dry decidious forests of the South Deccan plateau.

Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies

We have established a dedicated in-house field research initiative at our campus in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, to address critical gaps in knowledge about Eastern Ghats biodiversity, ecology, and conservation priorities.

Organic farming

A small percentage of land we own is allotted for farming where we grow paddy, pulses, millets and vegetables.

Farmer's Collective

We work very closely with the nearby village of Chinnathamandrapalli. The villagers play a vital role in all the work we undertake. We have enabled a collective of women working towards value added products. They also manage our farm lands and campus.

Farmer's Collective

We promote land stewardship and sustainable farming by employing the local community and supporting a farmers collective to create value-added products. Our goal is to provide eco-friendly job opportunities to counter urban migration among the younger generation.

Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) - A forest restoration project in the Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu

# Restoration project

We are trying to restore the land to a good ecological health using the little pockets of healthy forests as a reference in knowing what kind of an ecosystem is possible here.

We are focusing primarily in active restoration in the form of collecting seeds from the forest remnants of this region as well as from nearby reserve forests in the ecoregion to raise a nursery and carry out planting.

We have raised more than a 130 species of native flora and 15,000 saplings. Once saplings are of a certain age they are planted in the land during the monsoon months. Once planted and mulched we rely mostly on the rains to take care that the saplings don't dry out.

Natural regeneration is also a process that takes place in the land as we are sufficiently close to the forest. High wildlife activity helps in ensuring that some seeds get dispersed in the land.

# Our vision

To restore ecological balance by nurturing native flora and enriching the biodiversity on the land. Using healthy forest pockets as our inspiration, we’re developing a sustainable ecosystem that can thrive with minimal intervention.

#### Seed Collection and Nursery

Using seeds sourced from local forest remnants and nearby reserve forests, we cultivate over 100 species of native flora and currently have around 15,000 saplings. Each seedling is cared for in trays, pots, and bags until they reach planting maturity.

#### Planting Process

During the monsoon, mature saplings are transplanted and mulched on the land, relying mostly on natural rain for sustenance. We also see some natural regeneration due to high wildlife activity, as animals help disperse seeds.

# The Ecoregion

Our site is nestled in the unique Deccan Dry Deciduous Forest ecoregion, where deciduous and evergreen trees thrive alongside a wide range of shrubs and climbers. As we explore the secluded hills around the site, we uncover remnants of what once were lush forests, hinting at the ecological richness we aim to restore.

#### Flora Diversity

We encounter a diverse array of trees including Chloroxylon swietenia, Diospyros montana, Wrightia tinctoria, and Ficus tsjahela, which are native to this area. These species form a vital part of the dense canopy in less disturbed areas and are essential for ecological balance.

#### Fauna in the Region

The land is also a natural habitat for an impressive range of fauna including the Sloth Bear, Amur Falcon, Indian Rock Python, and Asian Elephant. The diversity of wildlife plays a critical role in sustaining this ecosystem.

# Volunteering at EBTL

Join us in our journey towards a greener, richer ecosystem. By nurturing these lands and reintroducing native species, we hope to restore the ecological balance that once thrived here.

Write to [email protected] to know more

import requests, json, math

lat, lon = 12.733937, 78.183437
# 70 acres ≈ 0.283 km²; approximate site radius ~300-400m if elongated
# Query amphibians within ~2km and within ~10km for regional pool

def gbif(bbox=None, lat=None, lon=None, radius_km=None, limit=300):
    params = {
        'classKey': 131,  # Amphibia
        'hasCoordinate': 'true',
        'limit': limit,
        'offset': 0,
    }
    if bbox:
        params['decimalLatitude'] = f"{bbox[0]},{bbox[2]}"
        params['decimalLongitude'] = f"{bbox[1]},{bbox[3]}"
        # GBIF uses separate min/max
        params = {
            'classKey': 131,
            'hasCoordinate': 'true',
            'limit': limit,
            'decimalLatitude': f'{bbox[0]},{bbox[2]}',
            'decimalLongitude': f'{bbox[1]},{bbox[3]}',
        }
    url = 'https://api.gbif.org/v1/occurrence/search'
    # Better: use geoDistance or bounding box properly
    params = {
        'classKey': '131',
        'hasCoordinate': 'true',
        'limit': str(limit),
        'occurrenceStatus': 'PRESENT',
    }
    if radius_km is not None:
        params['geoDistance'] = f'{lat},{lon},{radius_km}km'
    else:
        # minLat,maxLat,minLon,maxLon via decimalLatitude/Longitude ranges
        min_lat, min_lon, max_lat, max_lon = bbox
        params['decimalLatitude'] = f'{min_lat},{max_lat}'
        params['decimalLongitude'] = f'{min_lon},{max_lon}'
    r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

# Site-scale ~0.5 km, local 2 km, landscape 10 km, district 25 km
for name, rk in [('0.5km',0.5),('2km',2),('5km',5),('10km',10),('25km',25)]:
    data = gbif(lat=lat, lon=lon, radius_km=rk, limit=300)
    print(f'\n=== Amphibia within {name}: count={data.get("count")} ===')
    spp = {}
    for o in data.get('results', []):
        sp = o.get('species') or o.get('scientificName') or 'unknown'
        spp[sp] = spp.get(sp, 0) + 1
    for sp, n in sorted(spp.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:25]:
        print(f'  {n:3d}  {sp}')

# Also Anura order specifically
print('\n=== Checking order Anura via taxonKey ===')
# Anura taxonKey = 952
for rk in [2, 10, 25]:
    r = requests.get('https://api.gbif.org/v1/occurrence/search', params={
        'taxonKey': 952,
        'hasCoordinate': 'true',
        'geoDistance': f'{lat},{lon},{rk}km',
        'limit': 300,
        'occurrenceStatus': 'PRESENT',
    }, timeout=60)
    data = r.json()
    print(f'Anura {rk}km: count={data.get("count")}')
    spp = {}
    coords = []
    for o in data.get('results', []):
        sp = o.get('species') or o.get('scientificName')
        spp[sp] = spp.get(sp, 0) + 1
        coords.append((o.get('decimalLatitude'), o.get('decimalLongitude'), sp, o.get('year'), o.get('datasetName')))
    for sp, n in sorted(spp.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:20]:
        print(f'  {n:3d}  {sp}')
    # show closest points
    def dist(a,b):
        # rough km
        return math.hypot((a[0]-lat)*111, (a[1]-lon)*111*math.cos(math.radians(lat)))
    closest = sorted(coords, key=lambda c: dist(c, (lat,lon)))[:15]
    print('  Closest:')
    for c in closest:
        print(f'    {dist(c,(lat,lon)):5.2f}km  {c[2]}  {c[3]}  {c[0]},{c[1]}  {c[4]}')
PY

**Best estimate: frogs regularly use about 25–40% of EBTL (~7–11 ha), almost entirely the northern wetland–lake complex; core breeding water is only ~10–15% of the site (~3–4.5 ha).** Public databases understate this because of sampling bias, not because the land is frog-empty.

---

### Site and data used

| Item | Value | Source |
|------|--------|--------|
| Site | Elephants By The Lake (EBTL), ~68–70 acres (~28 ha) | [ebtl.earth](https://ebtl.earth/) |
| Location | Plus Code **7J4WP5MM+H9**, Budhimutlu / Chinna Tammaradapalli, Krishnagiri, TN 635121 | Site footer; Nominatim reverse geocode |
| Coordinates | **12.734°N, 78.183°E** | Open Location Code decode of `P5MM+H9` |
| Habitats | N: percolation ponds, wetland, panchayat lake; mid: living space, nursery/garden; S: restoration/wild zones next to Veppanapalli RF | [EBTL site map](https://ebtl.earth/static/images/ebtl-map-new.png) |
| Satellite check | Central tank/lake, small N pond, open scrub W/N, denser cover SE | ESRI World Imagery export around the Plus Code |

---

### Why public DBs look empty (but frogs are there)

**GBIF (Anura, research-grade / indexed occurrences):**

- **0** records within **2 km** of the Plus Code  
- **16** within **5 km**, **18** within **10 km**, **69** within **25 km**  
- Nearby species pool: *Hoplobatrachus tigerinus*, *Uperodon taprobanicus*, *Uperodon systoma*, *Uperodon variegatus*, *Sphaerotheca rolandae/breviceps*, *Euphlyctis cyanophlyctis*, *Polypedates maculatus*, *Microhyla ornata/rubra*, *Minervarya agricola*, *Duttaphrynus melanostictus*  
- Query: `https://api.gbif.org/v1/occurrence/search` with `taxonKey=952` and `geoDistance=12.733937,78.183437,{r}km`

**iNaturalist (Amphibia, all grades):**

- **5** obs within **0.5 km**, **8** within **2 km** — including on-campus  
- Examples on/near site: *Minervarya agricola* at place guess **P5MM+H9** ([obs 332000489](https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/332000489)); *Microhyla ornata*, *Uperodon systoma*, *Polypedates maculatus* within ~0.3–0.4 km (Aug–Dec 2024–2025)  
- Most are `needs_id`, so they **do not** flow into GBIF research-grade — that is why GBIF looks empty inside the fence

So sparse public records ≠ low occupancy; they reflect few research-grade uploads and nocturnal under-sampling.

---

### Occupancy estimate (method you can re-run)

**1. Map area (schematic)**  
On the published EBTL map, wetland/teal aquatic pixels were ~**15%** of mapped land colors → **~4.3 ha (~11 acres)** if applied to 69 acres. Aquatic cover is concentrated in the **northern third** of the elongated site (south ≈ dry restoration).

**2. Ecological buffer (dry-zone anurans)**  
Eastern Ghats / Deccan dry-deciduous frogs cluster on standing water and use a short terrestrial halo (litter, bunds, shrubs), especially after rain ([Gingee Hills inventory](http://www.ajcb.in/journals/full_papers_july_2018/AJCB-Vol7-No1-Karthik%20et%20al.pdf); Nallamala habitat typology; Meghamalai dry-forest anuran lists).  

Treating wetland+lake ≈ **3.5–4.5 ha** core, plus a **50–100 m** activity buffer, yields roughly **8–12 ha** of high-use habitat ≈ **29–43%** of the property — nearly all **north of the nursery / learning centre**.

**3. Seasonal nuance**

| Zone | Approx. share of site | Frog use |
|------|----------------------|----------|
| Wetland + percolation ponds + lake | ~10–15% | Core breeding / calling; year-round if water holds |
| N terrestrial fringe (≤~100 m from water), nursery irrigation | ~15–25% | Night foraging, calling from edges |
| Mid campus (lights, drains) | small | Opportunistic (*Duttaphrynus*, *Polypedates*) |
| S restoration / wild | ~½ of site | Low in dry months; **burrowing frogs after monsoon rain** |

**Verdict to use in planning:** report **~⅓ of the site occupied under normal wet-season nights**, with **breeding effectively confined to the northern aquatic complex (~⅛ of area)**. Do not treat the whole 70 acres as frog habitat.

---

### Where next night surveys should go (priority order)

1. **Panchayat lake shoreline** — full circuit; focus shallow, vegetated, and muddy edges (*Hoplobatrachus*, *Euphlyctis*, *Minervarya*).  
2. **Wetland interior + three percolation ponds** (north tip) — walk slowly; listen for *Microhyla* / *Uperodon*; check for eggs/tadpoles.  
3. **Wetland–campus ecotone** (learning centre / living space drains and lit edges) — short station for *Duttaphrynus* and *Polypedates*.  
4. **Nursery / food-garden irrigation margins** after watering or rain — *Minervarya*, small microhylids.  
5. **Only after heavy rain:** southern restoration patches and **SE edge toward Veppanapalli RF** — *Sphaerotheca*, *Uperodon* emerging from burrows; *Polypedates* on shrubs.

**Protocol (checkable):** time-constrained visual encounter + acoustic (e.g. 3–4 × 30–45 min stations), **19:00–23:00**, peak from local phenology **Aug–Nov** (matches on-site iNat dates). Record presence by station, water permanence, and GPS — then you can replace this habitat prior with an empirical occupancy model. Upload research-grade IDs so GBIF catches up.

---

### Bottom line

Frogs at EBTL are a **northern aquatic problem**, not a whole-property one: expect **~10–15% core water habitat** and **~25–40% regular night-use area**. Put survey effort on the **lake–wetland–pond complex first**; use the southern wild zones mainly as **post-rain** secondary transects.The background habitat run finished successfully: on the EBTL schematic map, aquatic/wetland colors were about **15%** of mapped land (~**4.3 ha** of the ~69-acre site), concentrated in the north. That underpins the occupancy estimate already given — frogs mainly use the northern lake–wetland–pond complex, so night surveys should start there.
